source.title: A Random Matrix Perspective of Echo State Networks: From Precise Bias--Variance Characterization to Optimal Regularization
source.authors: Yessin Moakher; Malik Tiomoko; Cosme Louart; Zhenyu Liao

record.file_problem: The text contains the full paper, though some figure labels and plotted values are garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes double descent in ESNs and compares them with ridge regression, concluding that ESNs generally do not exhibit double descent while ridge regression does.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 and its accompanying discussion report test-error behavior across the context-length-to-sample-size ratio. Figure 3 compares ridge and ESN errors across training size but does not state that increasing sample size raises test error near interpolation. Figure 4 tests an optimal-regularization formula, not whether tuning removes a double-descent peak.
record.test_reason: An asymptotic random-matrix analysis plus experiments sweeping T/N (feature dimension over samples). It argues that linear ESNs do not show the double-descent peak that ridge regression shows at T≈N. The peak is tied to an effective-complexity quantity α approaching 1. This bears on V4 (a non-deep model class) and on V5 (a single complexity measure locating the peak). It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that linear ESNs avoid double descent because the leak factor yields a low-rank spectrum that keeps α below 1, while ridge regression peaks at T≈N as λ→0. They allow an exception for degenerate regimes (φ=1, vanishing λ). They also find that ESNs beat ridge regression when data are scarce and the task relies on recent inputs, and they derive an optimal λ*=(T/N)·SNR.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an asymptotic random-matrix analysis and experiments on teacher–student linear ESNs and ridge regression, rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis says ESN behavior depends on the leak factor and regularization; double descent may occur in degenerate regimes with no leakage (phi = 1) and vanishing regularization. The plotted comparisons vary teacher-memory parameter rho.
record.problems: The plotted values are not recoverable from the extracted figure text, and the paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the plotted comparisons. The experimental comparison is limited to ridge regression and linear ESNs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure 3 reports ridge–ESN error differences across training size, but the text does not report a rise in test error as sample size increases near interpolation. Figure 4 reports validation of the optimal-regularization formula, not double-descent behavior under tuned regularization.

untested.parts: Fig. 3 varies N but shows only ridge–ESN differences, not a rise in test error with more samples near interpolation.
Only ridge regression and linear ESNs are studied. Nonlinear ESNs, other RNNs and broader model classes are left to future work.
Only the T/N axis is tested. Epochs and an explicit sample-size axis are not, and α is a ridge-specific quantity, not a general EMC.
Noise-driven peaks, multiple peaks and removal of the peak under optimal λ are not tested. Fig. 4 only validates the λ* formula.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Theoretical statement that ESNs regain double descent in the degenerate regime with no leakage (φ=1) and vanishing regularization, and that the ridge peak requires λ→0. This is a regularization-dependence condition with no row.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence is figure-only, with no numbers or uncertainty given. The λ and φ used for Fig. 2 are not stated. The ridge double descent is a reproduction of known linear-regression theory. The ESN result is the novel finding. α plays a role akin to effective complexity but is defined for ridge-type readouts only.

versions.untested_parts: Whether increasing training samples near interpolation raises test error.
The study analyzes linear ESNs and ridge regression, not a broad range of model classes.
The effective-complexity account is discussed for the context-length/sample-size ratio; no unified prediction is tested across size, epochs, and sample-size axes.
The study does not test noise-driven peaks, multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a double-descent peak.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective parameter count and test whether that turns double descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
